title: What If You Fired a Gun in Space? The Bullet Could Come Back for You

scenes.text: What if you fired a gun in space? The bullet never stops. And it might come back.
First, it works. Modern cartridges carry their own oxygen in the powder, so the gun fires without air.
The smoke doesn't trail behind. It expands from the barrel as a perfect sphere.
The bullet leaves at about 1,000 metres a second. You drift backwards at a few centimetres a second, forever.
With nothing to slow it, the bullet coasts for millions of years. Fire it sideways in orbit and, with perfect aim, it circles the planet and hits you from behind.
Point it at Jupiter instead, and gravity drags it in at nearly 60 kilometres a second. The only known gun ever fired in space was a cannon on a Soviet station, in 1975.

description:
What if you fired a gun in space? Modern ammunition carries its own oxidizer, so it fires in a vacuum; the smoke forms an expanding sphere, the bullet leaves at about 1,000 metres per second, and recoil pushes you back at a few centimetres per second with nothing to stop you.
Astronomers told Space.com the bullet would coast almost forever: fired horizontally in orbit with perfect aim, it could circle a planet and strike the shooter from behind, and aimed at Jupiter it would be pulled in at nearly 60 kilometres per second. The only known gun fired in space was a 23 mm cannon on the Soviet Salyut 3 station in January 1975.
What should we run through next?
first_comment: Cosmonauts really carried a survival gun on Soyuz flights, but for bears after landing in Siberia, not for space. What would you fire into orbit? Drop your own what-if below.
